analysis.one_liner: Phases out private, for-profit federal prisons and halfway houses.
analysis.headline: The bill, which attracted no cosponsors, died in a House subcommittee without ever getting a hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar the Bureau of Prisons and the U.S. Marshals Service from hiring private, for-profit companies to run federal prisons, with a six-year phase-out, and would bar for-profit companies from running federal halfway houses, with an eight-year phase-out [S3]. It would also require federal prisons to give released inmates counseling on things like expungement, job programs, food assistance, Medicaid, and voter registration [S3]. It never received any action beyond referral to committee.
analysis.who_benefits: People held in federal custody, who would be housed and supervised by direct federal employees rather than contractors, and people leaving federal prison, who would get help with jobs, benefits, expungement, and voting under the bill's reentry provisions [S3]. Federal prison workers would also gain, since core correctional work would have to be done by federal employees [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Federal inmates and people leaving prison

how_it_helps.text: After a six-year transition, all core correctional services at Bureau of Prisons and Marshals Service facilities would have to be performed by federal government employees; state and local government facilities could still be used, but for-profit contractors could not [S3].
Eight years after enactment, the Bureau of Prisons could no longer contract with any for-profit entity to run community confinement facilities such as halfway houses [S3].

Every released federal prisoner would receive information and counseling about expungement rights, job programs, vocational and educational rehabilitation, food assistance, Medicaid, Social Security, driver's licenses, and voter registration [S3].
The Marshals Service would have to inspect every facility it uses each year for compliance with constitutional and other standards [S3].

analysis.who_pays: For-profit prison and halfway house companies would lose federal contracts worth billions of dollars. Taxpayers could face transition costs if direct federal operation costs more than contracted beds, at least initially, and some towns whose economies depend on private prison facilities would lose jobs.
analysis.who_pays_short: For-profit prison contractors and host towns

drawbacks.text: The phase-out periods are long — six years for prisons and eight years for halfway houses — so the status quo would continue for most of a decade after enactment [S3].
Moving from contracted beds to direct federal operation could cost more in the short run, and towns built around private prison facilities would lose jobs when contracts end.
The bill only covers federal facilities, leaving private confinement under state and local systems untouched [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is straightforward: federal custody would no longer be delegated to companies paid per inmate, and people leaving prison would get concrete help reentering society. The main costs are transition spending and the long timelines, which soften the impact; the federal-only scope is a real limitation. On balance the design is reasonable, though it is more gradual than its title suggests.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to a crime subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended without a hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman introduced the bill on October 31, 2019, and it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee [S1] [S5].
On December 18, 2019, it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security, and no further action followed [S5].
No member of the House cosponsored the bill [S4].
The bill received no hearing, committee markup, or floor vote before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For-profit prison and community confinement companies kept their federal contracts and revenue, since nothing changed; the decades-long status quo of contracted federal confinement continued. People in federal custody gained nothing from the bill's reentry and inspection provisions, which never became law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private prison contractors kept their contracts

for.name: Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to phase out for-profit federal prisons and halfway houses; attracted no cosponsors.

against.name: Rep. Jerrold Nadler
against.what_they_did: The committee referred the bill to a subcommittee and never scheduled a hearing or markup, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Private prison and community confinement contractors
against.role: Operators of federal contracted prisons and halfway houses
against.what_they_did: Had a direct financial stake in keeping federal contracts; the federal contracting system for private confinement continued unchanged through the bill's death.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no Republican or other Democrat cosponsored the bill, so the partisan shape of the opposition never showed up in the record; the bill simply stalled in committee with a Democratic majority.

industries.note: Companies like CoreCivic and GEO Group run Bureau of Prisons and Marshals Service facilities under contracts; the bill would have ended that revenue after a six-year phase-out. Their business model depends on incarceration — the more people confined and the longer, the more they earn — which runs against the interest of people in custody and the public paying for it.

industries.industry: For-profit community confinement and halfway house operators
industries.note: The bill would bar the Bureau of Prisons from contracting with for-profit entities to run halfway houses after eight years, eliminating that line of business for federal cases.

industries.industry: Federal prison workforce (correctional officers and BOP employees)
industries.note: Core correctional work — housing, safeguarding, and discipline of inmates — would have to be done by federal employees, shifting work from contractors to the federal workforce. Public interest in who runs prisons and worker interest in the jobs largely line up here.
